passage:
Family counselling note, 3 March. Jahnavi, 25, came alone today. Her father's two acres near Nashik are to be divided between her and her brother Yogesh. Yogesh now wants the half with the well and the road frontage, saying that as the son who stayed nearby, he deserves more.

Jahnavi's voice shook as she described their last call. "He said I was greedy for even asking. Me!" She kept pressing her thumbnail into her palm. She said she felt betrayed, and that she was ready never to speak to him again.

I asked whether she wanted the land settled or the brother lost. She was quiet a long time. "The land settled. I don't want to lose him."

We agreed on next steps: she will ask her mother's cousin, whom both siblings respect, to sit with them as a neutral elder, and consult a lawyer so any agreement is written down. She will not reply to Yogesh while angry.

qa.q: What does Yogesh want from the two acres?
qa.a: He wants the half with the well and the road frontage.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling as she described the call?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt angry and betrayed, pressing her thumbnail into her palm, ready never to speak to him again.

qa.q: Which next steps did Jahnavi agree to, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Bringing in a respected neutral elder and a lawyer so the agreement is written down, and not replying while angry, protects both the land and the relationship.

qa.q: How does Yogesh seem to see his claim?
qa.a: Yogesh seems to feel he has earned more by staying nearby, and he sees Jahnavi's request as greed.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman whose brother pushes for a bigger share of family land, feeling angry and betrayed, choosing a neutral elder, written terms and repair over a cut-off.

Thursday, late.

Ujjwal came over after dinner with a folder. He'd already got a broker to value Mummy's flat. "Didi, you're married, you're settled. I need seventy percent to start the business. It's only fair." Fair. I actually laughed, and then I couldn't stop shaking.

This is my little brother. I taught him to ride a cycle in that building's parking. And he'd gone to a broker before he came to me.

I nearly said, "Take the whole flat and never call me again." I didn't. I said I needed time and walked him to the door.

Things I decided at 1 a.m.:
- Nothing gets agreed on the phone or in anger.
- I'll ask Madhav mama to sit with us both. He's fair and Ujjwal listens to him.
- Whatever we decide goes in writing, with a lawyer.
- I will not cut him off over one flat.

Still furious. Still his Didi. — Minakshi

qa.q: What had Ujjwal done before coming to his sister?
qa.a: He had already got a broker to value Mummy's flat.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling after Ujjwal showed her the folder?
qa.a: Minakshi felt angry and betrayed, shaking and hurt that he went to a broker before coming to her.

qa.q: What plan did Minakshi make, and why does it help?
qa.a: No deals in anger, a fair elder to mediate, everything in writing with a lawyer, and no cut-off; it lets her protect herself while keeping the relationship possible.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see his request?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems to believe it is fair because his sister is settled and he needs money for a business.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young woman whose younger brother pushes for a bigger share of family property, feeling angry and betrayed, choosing an elder, written terms and not cutting him off.

Sunday. Ammi's birthday lunch.

Faisal got a new watch from Abbu. In front of everyone. "For my son who makes me proud." I got a pat on the shoulder. I've been sending half my salary home for three years. Faisal still borrows from them.

I smiled through the biryani, then went and sat on the stairs for a while so no one would see my face. I felt invisible, like the extra chair at the table.

What I'm not going to do: pick a fight with Faisal. It's not his watch that hurts. It's Abbu's words.

What I might do: talk to Ammi quietly next week, maybe on our evening walk. Just say, "I felt unseen today." No accusations.

In the evening I went to cricket with Pankaj and the office team. I hit two fours and everyone cheered like idiots. That helped more than I expected.

I'm Wasim, their son too. I'm allowed to be enough without the watch.

qa.a: He gave Faisal a new watch.

I'm Kamal, Anjali's big brother, and when you asked what I learned this year, it's this: loving someone doesn't give you the steering wheel.

Anjali is five years younger. When she said she was leaving her bank job to do theatre in Mumbai, I had a whole speech ready. Rent, no pension, what people would say. I even made her a spreadsheet. I really believed I was protecting her.

She listened, then said, "Bhaiya, you're not asking what I want. You're telling me what you're scared of."

That stung, because it was true. My fear felt like love from the inside.

So I tried something different. I asked her what the first year would look like. I helped her move boxes. I went to her first show, sat in the third row, and clapped like a madman. She's struggling with rent. I've told her I'm here if she wants to talk it through. The decision stays hers.

qa.q: What job did Anjali leave to do theatre?
qa.a: She left her bank job.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he made the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Kamal felt protective and scared for his sister, believing his fear was love.

qa.q: What changed in how Kamal supported Anjali?
qa.a: He stopped steering and started asking what she wanted, helping her move, attending her show and offering to listen while leaving the decisions to her.

qa.q: How did Anjali see Kamal's speech and spreadsheet?
qa.a: Anjali saw it as him telling her his fears instead of asking what she wanted, which felt controlling.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young man protective of his younger sister starting her life, who learns to support and listen and accepts her choices as her own.

Friday. Bhavna announced over dinner that she was leaving her IT job to open a home bakery. Chandrika put her fork down. "You're twenty-three. You'll lose everything." She spent the next hour listing risks. Bhavna went to bed without saying goodnight, and Chandrika lay awake, heart racing, sure she had to stop her little sister from ruining her life.

Tuesday. Bhavna's message was short. "Di, I need a sister, not a manager." Chandrika read it on the metro three times. Her hands felt cold. Was she doing to Bhavna what their father had done to her?

Two weeks later. Chandrika came to the first bake sale in the society courtyard. She didn't mention the job once. She helped carry trays, asked which cake Bhavna was proudest of, and bought two. When Bhavna asked, "Do you still think it's a mistake?" Chandrika said, "I'm scared for you. But it's your life, and I'm on your side."

qa.q: What did Bhavna plan to open?
qa.a: She planned to open a home bakery.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel reading Bhavna's message on the metro?
qa.a: Chandrika felt shaken and uneasy, her hands cold, wondering if she was repeating their father's control.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do differently at the bake sale?
qa.a: She dropped the lecture, helped, asked what Bhavna was proud of, and was honest about her fear while accepting the choice was Bhavna's.

qa.q: How did Bhavna experience her sister's first reaction?
qa.a: Bhavna felt managed and hurt, going to bed without saying goodnight and later asking for a sister, not a manager.

grounding: The story shows an older sister protective of her younger sibling's new path, moving from control to support over two weeks and accepting that the choices are her sister's.

In Rajni's village outside Hassan, the milk van came at six, and so, one Sunday, did her younger sister Jaya, off the first bus from town with swollen eyes.

They sat on the back step with coffee. "Akka, I need you to be honest. Not nice. Honest." Jaya had been offered a transfer to Hubli, but her husband didn't want to move, and she did. "Everyone else will just say, 'Listen to your husband' or 'Do what you like.' You always tell me the truth."

Rajni felt warm right through. As children she had bossed Jaya around endlessly, and Jaya had sulked her way out of chores. Now she was being asked, not obeyed.

She said what she thought: that the move mattered, and that Jaya had to talk to her husband before deciding anything. Jaya nodded slowly.

"And Akka, don't tell Amma yet." Rajni didn't. When Amma asked why Jaya had come, she said, "Just to see me."

qa.q: How did Jaya reach the village that Sunday?
qa.a: She came off the first bus from town.

qa.q: What did Rajni feel when Jaya asked for her honesty?
qa.a: Rajni felt warm, glad and trusted, being asked rather than obeyed.

qa.q: How did Rajni avoid slipping into her old role?
qa.a: She gave an honest opinion without bossing Jaya, left the decision with Jaya and her husband, and kept the confidence from Amma.

qa.q: How does Jaya see her older sister now?
qa.a: Jaya sees Rajni as the one person who will tell her the truth, not just what she wants to hear.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman whose younger sister turns to her for honesty as an adult, feeling glad and needed, keeping her confidence and avoiding the old bossy role.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,

It's been three weeks since Abbu. I'm writing because every time we talk, we end up hurting each other.

When you went back to the shop two days after the funeral, I thought you didn't care. I said so, and I'm sorry. Last night Ammi told me you sit in his chair at the counter after closing, in the dark. I didn't know.

Maybe you think I'm dramatic. I cry at the dhaba where he used to take us, at the smell of his attar, at nothing. I think we're both grieving; we just do it differently.

So, a question, not an accusation: how are you managing, really?

And a memory, because I keep thinking of it: Abbu teaching us to count change with his old brass coins, you always cheating.

The papers about the shop can wait. Let's not decide anything until the first wave of this has passed.

Your sister,
Hafsa

qa.q: How long after the funeral did Yusuf go back to the shop?
qa.a: He went back to the shop two days after the funeral.

qa.q: What did Hafsa feel when she learned Yusuf sits in Abbu's chair after closing?
qa.a: Hafsa felt sorry and softened, realising his quiet was his way of grieving and that she had misjudged him.

qa.a: She apologises, asks how he is coping, shares a memory, and delays the shop papers until the first wave of grief has passed.

qa.a: Yusuf probably felt hurt and misunderstood, since he was grieving privately in the dark shop.

grounding: A letter shows a young woman and her brother grieving their father differently and misreading each other, who asks how he is coping, shares a memory and delays settling assets.

You asked me at this group to say why I came. I'm Harish. My mother died in August, and I think I lost my sister for a while too.

Gargi cried for days. She called me at midnight, played Amma's voice notes, wanted to talk about everything. I couldn't. I cleaned Amma's cupboards, cancelled her phone, filed papers. Gargi said her brother had turned into a machine. I thought she was making it harder for everyone.

Then, in October, I found Amma's recipe notebook and sat on the kitchen floor for an hour. I called Gargi. Not about papers. I just said, "How are you actually doing?"

She was quiet, then said, "I thought you didn't miss her." I said, "I miss her so much I can't stop tidying."

Now we cook one of Amma's recipes together every Sunday. We've agreed the house can wait until next year.

qa.a: He found Amma's recipe notebook.

The staffroom at the girls' school had emptied for the bell, and Chandrika sat with Gargi's message open on her phone. "Can't make it to Mummy's birthday. Fees for my course are due, working extra shifts."

Chandrika thought of her MBA certificate, framed in her parents' hall. Papa had paid for all of it, and for her wedding. When it was Gargi's turn, the money had run out, and Gargi had taken a loan for a diploma instead. Chandrika had never once said anything about it. It made her stomach twist.

She thought of sending a huge cheque. That would be easy, and it would buy her out of the feeling.

Instead she typed: "Gargi, I got far more support from Mummy-Papa than you did. I've known it for years and never said it. I'm sorry. I'd like to cover this semester's fees, and I'd like to talk properly on Sunday."

The next bell rang. Three dots appeared.

qa.a: Papa had paid for all of it.

qa.a: Chandrika felt guilty, her stomach twisting, knowing she had received much more support.

Dear Shalini,

I'm writing this instead of saying it because I'd lose my nerve.

When Appa got sick, you gave up your hostel seat in Coimbatore to come home and help. I stayed in Chennai and finished my degree. Appa and Amma kept sending me money for the flat, even when there wasn't much. I told myself it was fine. It wasn't.

For years I've felt guilty whenever we talk, and so we've talked less and less. That's the worst of it: my guilt made me distant from the person I owe the most.

I'm sorry. You carried what I didn't.

I'd like to do something fair. I can pay for the evening course you mentioned, and I'll take Appa's hospital visits every other month from now on. I'm not trying to buy back the past. I just want us to be sisters again, the way we were before.

Tell me honestly what you think.

Sudha

qa.a: Shalini gave up her hostel seat in Coimbatore.

qa.a: Sudha has felt guilty whenever they talk, which made her pull away and grow distant from her sister.

qa.q: What makes Sudha's offer fair rather than over-giving?

grounding: A letter shows a young woman who took more than her share of family support, feeling guilty, acknowledging it honestly and offering fair, specific repair.

The vaccination room at the urban health centre was full of crying babies, and Anjali's son was the loudest. She had slept maybe three hours in two days. When the nurse asked for his card, Anjali realised she had left it at home and burst into tears.

"I can't even remember a card. I'm failing him."

Another mother on the bench, holding twins, patted her arm. "Every one of us here feels that."

The nurse, kind but busy, said, "We'll write it in again. How are you sleeping? How is your mood?"

"Low. All the time."

"Then tell your doctor at the next check-up, and don't wait if it stays like this. Who helps you at home?"

That evening Anjali said to Omkar, "I need you to take the 2 a.m. feed, and your mother to come on Tuesdays. And the house can be messy." Omkar nodded and set his alarm.

In Jyoti's village near Jhansi, the temple steps were steep and worn smooth, and little Lavanya wanted to climb them all by herself.

Jyoti's heart jumped every time the girl's foot wobbled. Last month a boy from the next lane had fallen into the pond, and since then Jyoti had carried Lavanya everywhere, even though she was two and could walk perfectly well.

"Let her," said the old flower-seller at the bottom. "How else will her legs learn?"

Jyoti bit her lip. Then she knelt one step below her daughter and kept her hand close, not holding. Lavanya climbed, puffing, knees black with dust. One step. Two. At the top she turned around and shouted, "Amma! Me!" with her arms in the air.

Jyoti laughed, and her eyes stung. Coming down, she held Lavanya's hand only on the broken step. At the pond, she still kept a firm grip.

qa.q: How old was Lavanya?
qa.a: Lavanya was two.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as Lavanya began to climb?
qa.a: Jyoti felt fearful and protective, her heart jumping at every wobble after the boy's fall into the pond.

qa.q: How did Jyoti balance safety and freedom?
qa.a: She stayed one step below with her hand close but not holding, held on only at the broken step, and kept a firm grip at the pond where the danger was real.

qa.q: What was the climb like for Lavanya?
qa.a: It was hard but thrilling, and reaching the top made her proud, shouting "Amma! Me!"

At the playground in Valencia, eighteen-month-old Lucas headed for the small climbing frame, and his father Mateo was there before him, arms out like a goalkeeper.

"He's fine," said Jamal from the bench, rocking his own daughter's pushchair. "The drop is about thirty centimetres."

"He could hit his head."

"He could. On the soft mat."

Mateo laughed, but his shoulders stayed tight. Since the night Lucas had been born early and spent a week in the hospital, every edge in the world looked sharp to him.

He took one step back. Then another. Lucas grabbed the rail, got one knee up, slipped, sat down hard on the mat, looked surprised, and tried again. On the third try he made it and slapped the top bar, grinning.

Mateo's chest ached with pride and leftover fear. "Okay," he admitted to Jamal. "I nearly ruined that."

qa.q: How old was Lucas?
qa.a: Lucas was eighteen months old.

qa.q: Why did every edge look sharp to Mateo?
qa.a: Mateo felt fiercely protective and still frightened since Lucas was born early and spent a week in hospital.

Before: a Wednesday in March. Lokesh and Aparna passed each other in the hallway like shift workers. "Did you give her the drops?" "I told you I did." "You didn't write it down." The baby was four months old and they had not had a conversation that wasn't about nappies in weeks. That night Lokesh slept on the sofa, angry and lonely at once.

During: the following Sunday. Lokesh made a chart on the fridge: night feeds split, his nights Monday, Wednesday, Friday. Then he said the harder thing. "I miss you. Not the mother of our daughter. You." Aparna's face crumpled and she laughed. "I thought you were just annoyed with me."

After: three weeks later. Every evening after the baby slept, they took ten minutes on the balcony, no phones. Lokesh said "Thank you" out loud for small things, and so did she. They still bickered sometimes. But now they bickered as a team.

Arnab, you think your Yamini dida doesn't understand? When your father was born, your grandfather and I nearly stopped speaking.

We lived in two rooms in Howrah. The baby cried from nine till three every night. Your dadu worked at the mill, I did everything else, and we started keeping score. "I was up at one." "I was up at two and four." We spoke like two clerks handing over a ledger.

One night I snapped and threw a steel glass at the wall. Not at him, at the wall. We both stood there shocked.

The next morning, he brought me tea in bed, which he had never done. He said, "Yamini, we're on the same side." We sat for ten minutes before the baby woke. We decided he'd take the baby from nine to midnight, I'd take the rest. And we made a rule: every night, one thank-you, out loud.

We kept that rule for fifty-one years.

qa.q: Where did Yamini and her husband live when the baby was born?
qa.a: They lived in two rooms in Howrah.

qa.q: How did young Yamini feel on the night she threw the glass?
qa.a: She felt exhausted, angry and cut off from her husband, and then shocked at herself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yamini's story?
qa.a: The morning her husband brought tea and said they were on the same side, after which they split the nights and began one thank-you a night.

qa.q: How might Yamini's husband have felt when the glass hit the wall?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and shaken, and it seems to have made him see how strained they had become.

Thomas and Bhavna sat in the paediatric clinic's waiting room with Anya asleep in the carrier when Thomas's mother called for the third time that day.

"Ask the doctor about starting rice water. At four months we gave you rice water." Then Bhavna's phone lit up: her mother, saying the baby must sleep on her tummy "or her head will go flat".

Bhavna closed her eyes. "I feel like I'm being graded, Thomas. Every day."

"Me too," he said. "Let's just ask Dr. Fernandes. Then we decide. Us."

The doctor was clear: no rice water yet, and babies sleep on their backs. On the way out, Thomas called his mother. "Thanks, Mummy. The doctor wants to wait on food. We'll tell you when." Bhavna texted her mother a thank-you and a photo of Anya on her back, sleeping. Her mother replied with a heart. Bhavna exhaled for the first time that morning.

qa.a: She said they gave him rice water at four months.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel as the calls and messages came in?
qa.a: Bhavna felt judged and tense, as if she was being graded every day.

qa.q: How did Thomas and Bhavna handle the advice well?
qa.a: They thanked both mothers, checked with their doctor, and made the decision together instead of arguing or stewing.

qa.q: How might Thomas's mother feel after his call?
qa.a: She might feel respected because he thanked her, even if a little disappointed her advice wasn't taken.

grounding: The passage shows young parents receiving constant advice from their own parents and feeling judged, who thank them, check with the doctor and decide together.

passage:
Dear Mummy and Papa,

I'm writing because when we talk on the phone, I get prickly and say things I don't mean.

First, thank you. You've come every weekend since Kiara was born. You've cooked, you've washed, you've walked her up and down when she wouldn't settle. Ankita and I couldn't have done these months without you.

But I need to say something honestly. Every visit comes with a list: she's too thin, she should be swaddled tighter, we're spoiling her by picking her up. I know it comes from love. Still, I go to bed feeling judged, and Ankita has started dreading Saturdays.

So here's what we'd like. Tell us your ideas; some of them are really good, like the lullaby, which works every time. But Ankita and I will make the final decisions, together, with our doctor. Please trust us to love her.

See you Saturday. We'll make the tea this time.

Your son,
Suraj

qa.q: What does Suraj say works every time?
qa.a: The lullaby works every time.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel after his parents' visits?
qa.a: Suraj feels judged and prickly, even while grateful for all their help.

qa.q: How does Suraj's letter handle the advice wisely?
qa.a: It thanks his parents sincerely, keeps the ideas that help, and clearly says he and Ankita will decide together with their doctor.

qa.q: How has Ankita been affected by the constant advice?
qa.a: Ankita has started dreading Saturdays, which shows she feels judged too.

grounding: A letter shows a new father who feels judged by his parents' constant advice, thanking them, taking what helps, and deciding with his partner instead of stewing or shouting.
